title: A Trick To Staying Calm All Day Long
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores why trying hard to stay calm often backfires, creating tension rather than relieving it, and instead recommends visualization as a proven method for building genuine, effortless composure. He instructs teachers to list the specific moments during the school day that trigger stress — loud group work, misbehavior during instruction, an argumentative student — and then, before school each morning, spend a few quiet minutes visualizing themselves handling those exact moments calmly and successfully. He notes that visualization styles vary from person to person, all equally valid, and suggests even thirty seconds before students arrive is worthwhile. He also recommends closing with an exaggerated, even comically stressful scenario to build resilience through humor. Citing visualization's near-equivalence to actual practice, Linsin frames the technique as remarkably efficient: once done for the day, teachers don't need to think about it further, and calm behavior follows naturally.
points: Actively trying hard to stay calm often creates more tension, since it turns something meant to be effortless into an act of willpower.
Listing specific daily stress triggers is the first step toward building a genuine visualization practice.
A few minutes of morning visualization, imagining oneself handling stressful moments with composure, works even in as little as thirty seconds.
Ending a visualization session with an exaggerated, even comically stressful scenario builds resilience through humor.
Visualization has been shown to be nearly as effective as actual practice, and requires no ongoing effort once completed for the day.
quotes: You become a volcano simmering under the surface. Staying outwardly calm becomes an act of willpower rather than what it should be: A reflection of how you feel on the inside.
Now, before school begins each morning, sit quietly with your list and visualize yourself handling those moments calmly and successfully.

A great way to finish your visualization is to conjure up an outrageously—even comically—stressful situation, like a troop of Howler monkeys swinging through your door and windows, and then watching yourself handling it with aplomb.
Visualization has been shown to be nearly as effective as actual practice. And because you’re able to do it over and over again in a short period of time, it’s remarkably efficient.
You'll find yourself naturally handling things with grace and poise. You'll feel more prepared and confident and less hesitant.
